env.world: A fixed finite population of \(n\) labeled units with \(K\ge2\) treatment arms \(\mathcal A_K=\{1,\ldots,K\}\) and fixed binary potential outcomes. Nature fixes a complete labeled response schedule \(z=(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\in\mathcal T_K^n\), \(\mathcal T_K=\{0,1\}^{\mathcal A_K}\), and \(Y_i(a)=t_{i,a}\). The experimenter chooses, before the schedule is revealed, an arbitrary assignment law \(\mathcal D\in\Delta(\mathcal A_K^n)\) — dependence across units and zero allocation probabilities permitted — and observes \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=Y_i(A_i)\). Assignment is the only source of randomness. For a fixed nonzero zero-sum contrast \(c\in\mathbb R^K\) with \(\sum_a c_a=0\), support \(S_c=\{a:c_a\ne0\}\) and \(\ell_1\) norm \(L_c=\sum_a|c_a|\), the target is \(\tau_c(z)=n^{-1}\sum_i\sum_a c_at_{i,a}\in[-L_c/2,L_c/2]\). An estimator \(\widehat\tau\) is an arbitrary, possibly biased map of \((A_i,Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}})_{i=1}^n\) clipped to \([-L_c/2,L_c/2]\); the loss is design-based squared error \(R_n(\mathcal D,\widehat\tau;z)=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[(\widehat\tau-\tau_c(z))^2]\) and the value is \(\rho_n(c)=\inf_{\mathcal D,\widehat\tau}\max_{z}R_n\). The first-order constant is \(C_0(c)=L_c^2/4\), the contrast-weighted allocation is \(q_a^\star=|c_a|/L_c\) on \(S_c\), and the second-order sequence is \(d_n(c)=C_0(c)/n-\rho_n(c)\). No exposure-positivity, overlap, rank, or inverse condition is imposed on the unrestricted game; only the displayed independent upper procedures use \(q_a^\star>0\) on active arms.

env.world: The unit-permutation orbit (symmetrized) form of the same experiment. \(\mathfrak S_n\) acts simultaneously on schedules, assignments, and observed outcome vectors. Schedule orbits are the response-type count vectors \(m=(m_t)_{t\in\mathcal T_K}\in\mathcal M_{n,K}=\{m\in\mathbb Z_+^{\mathcal T_K}:\sum_t m_t=n\}\), with \(\tau_c(m)=n^{-1}\sum_t m_t\sum_a c_at_a\). Assignment orbits are the allocation counts \(r\in\mathcal R_{n,K}=\{r\in\mathbb Z_+^{\mathcal A_K}:\sum_a r_a=n\}\), so an invariant design is exactly a mixture \(\pi\in\Delta(\mathcal R_{n,K})\) of uniform assignments conditional on \(r\). Observed-data orbits are the pairs \((r,x)\) with arm-success counts \(x_a=\#\{i:A_i=a,\;Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=1\}\), and an invariant estimator is a map \(\delta(r,x)\in[-L_c/2,L_c/2]\). Writing \(h=(h_{t,a})\) for the response-type-by-arm contingency table and \(\mathcal H(m,r,x)\) for its feasible fiber, the orbit likelihood is \(P_m(x\mid r)=\bigl(\prod_a r_a!/n!\bigr)\sum_{h\in\mathcal H(m,r,x)}\prod_t m_t!/\prod_a h_{t,a}!\), and the finite \(2^K\)-response-type game value is \(G_n(c)=\inf_{\pi,\delta}\max_{m\in\mathcal M_{n,K}}\sum_r\pi_r\sum_x P_m(x\mid r)\{\delta(r,x)-\tau_c(m)\}^2\). All state, action, and observation sets are finite; zero allocation counts and the all-zero and all-one response types are retained.

env.world: The rational grid-action linear program attached to the orbit experiment. For a rational nonzero zero-sum contrast \(c\in\mathbb Q^K\) put \(h_c=L_c/2\) and let the estimator action grid be \(\Gamma_{M,c}=\{-h_c+jh_c/M:j=0,\ldots,2M\}\) (mesh \(h_c/M\), containing both endpoints and \(0\)); for the three-arm diagnostic contrast \(c^\dagger=(1,-1/2,-1/2)\), \(h_{c^\dagger}=1\) and \(\Gamma_{M,c^\dagger}=\Gamma_M=\{-1+j/M\}\). The program minimizes the epigraph variable \(u\ge0\) over \(\pi_r\ge0\) and joint design-action weights \(w_{r,x,g}\ge0\) subject to \(\sum_r\pi_r=1\), \(\sum_g w_{r,x,g}=\pi_r\) for every \((r,x)\), and \(\sum_{r,x,g}P_m(x\mid r)w_{r,x,g}\{g-\tau_c(m)\}^2\le u\) for every \(m\in\mathcal M_{n,K}\). Its value is \(\Lambda_{n,M}(c)\), and \(\Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger=\Lambda_{n,M}(c^\dagger)\) with \(\rho_n^\dagger=\rho_n(c^\dagger)\). Every index set is finite and, for rational \(c\), every objective and constraint coefficient is rational.

citations.authors: Timothy Sudijono, Edgar Dobriban, and Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen
citations.verbatim_statement: \begin{theorem}\label{thm:simplified_model_minimax_risk}\begin{equation}\label{eq:simplified_minimax_risk} r_n^* = \rho_n^* = \inf_f \sup_{\cl{I}_n} \E\left(f(p + \textsf{Bin}(r,1/2)) - \frac{p-q}{n} \right)^2.\end{equation} Moreover, there is a unique $f^*_n$ minimizing \eqref{eq:simplified_minimax_risk} and it is the posterior mean of $(p-q)/n$ under a least-favorable prior $\pi_n^*$ on $\cl{I}_n$. As a consequence, $f^*_n$ is admissible and $\rho_n^*$ is the Bayes risk of $\pi_n^*.$ \end{theorem} \begin{theorem}\label{thm:minimax_risk_reduction} Let $f_n^*$ be the function minimizing \eqref{eq:simplified_minimax_risk} in the reduced model. Then \begin{equation}\label{eq:minimax_risk_is_equal_to_simplified_minimax_risk}\inf_{\cl{A}, \hat \tau} \sup_{\cl{P} \in \set{0,1}^{2n}} R_n(\cl{A},\hat \tau) = \rho_n^*.\end{equation} A minimax procedure achieving the upper bound is given by Bernoulli$(1/2)$ randomization with corresponding estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\Opt}=f^*_n(\sum_{i=1}^n S_i)$. Furthermore, this procedure is admissible. \end{theorem} \begin{theorem}\label{thm:second_order_minimax_risk_behavior} Let $a_1^{\prime}$ be the largest negative zero of the derivative of the Airy function. The minimax risk satisfies \[\rho_n^* = \frac{1}{n} - \frac{C_A}{n^{4/3}} + o_n(n^{-4/3}),\] with $C_A = -4^{1/3}a_1^{\prime} = 1.617\dots$. \end{theorem}

citations.title: Optimal Experimental Design and Estimation when Potential Outcomes are Bounded
citations.verbatim_statement: We now consider the minimax problem without restricting the class of estimators. The main result shows that independent randomization remains optimal while the optimal estimator is generally nonlinear: \begin{theorem}\label{theorem1} For nonnegative integers $k,m$ with $k+m\leq N$, define $\theta_{k,m}=\frac{2k+m}{N}$ and $p_{k,m}(x)=2^{-m}\binom{m}{x-k}$, $x=0,\ldots,N$, where $\binom{m}{j}=0$ when $j\notin\{0,\ldots,m\}$. Let $\cK_N$ be the set of all such $(k,m)$ and define $\kappa_N = \min_{d=(d_0,\ldots,d_N)\in[0,2]^{N+1}} \max_{(k,m)\in\cK_N} \sum_{x=0}^N p_{k,m}(x)(d_x-\theta_{k,m})^2.$ Then, over all measurable estimators, $\inf_{(\delta,\hat\beta)}\sup_{Y(\cdot)\in[L,U]^{2N}}\E_\delta[(\hat\beta-\beta)^2]=(U-L)^2\kappa_N.$ A minimax procedure is independent random assignment, with the estimator $\hat\beta^*_{NL}=\hat\beta^*+(U-L)\sum_{x=0}^N(d_x^*-2x/N)p_x(Z)$, where $\hat\beta^*$ is the optimal affine estimator in Proposition 1, $d^*=(d_0^*,\dots,d_N^*)$ is any solution to the displayed minimax problem, $p_x(z)=Pr(\sum_i B_i=x)$ for $B_i\stackrel{ind}{\sim}Bernoulli(z_i)$, and $Z=(Z_i)_{i=1}^N$ with $Z_i=\frac12+\frac{(2D_i-1)(Y_i-\frac{U+L}{2})}{U-L}\in[0,1]$. \end{theorem}

The paper setup defines one binary treatment indicator per unit, hence two potential-outcome arms, and the theorem ranges over bounded schedules [L,U]^{2N}, all assignment-estimator pairs, and all measurable estimators.
